Cows and calves are bathed, decorated with colour, bells and garlands, fed green fodder and jaggery, and circled with a lamp; cow shelters (gaushalas) hold open days and receive gifts of fodder. In Braj the day is kept with Krishna as the cowherd and his flute, and at Nathdwara the Shrinathji image is dressed as a gopa. Children in Braj are dressed as Krishna and Balarama and go to the cowsheds.
rule: Gopashtami falls on Kartik Shukla Ashtami (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Udaya rule. Shukla paksha, so Purnimanta and Amanta agree.

name: Akshaya Navami (Amla Navami)
what: Akshaya Navami, or Amla Navami, on Kartik Shukla Navami is kept under the amla tree. Families worship the tree in the morning with water, turmeric, kumkum and thread wound around the trunk, cook and eat a meal in its shade, and give away food and amla fruit; the day is said to open the Satya Yuga and to make every gift undiminishing (akshaya). In Mathura and Vrindavan it is the day of the Vraja Mandal parikrama, and in Bengal it is Jagaddhatri Puja. Many keep a fast until the meal under the tree.
rule: Akshaya Navami (Amla Navami) falls on Kartik Shukla Navami (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Udaya rule. Shukla paksha, so Purnimanta and Amanta agree.

name: Dev Uthani Ekadashi (Prabodhini)
what: Dev Uthani Ekadashi, or Prabodhini and Devutthana Ekadashi, on Kartik Shukla Ekadashi is the day Vishnu is said to wake after four months of sleep, closing Chaturmas. Beside the Ekadashi fast, an image of Vishnu is woken in the evening with bells, conch, lamps and the call 'utho Deva', a rangoli of his footprints is drawn from the door, and sugarcane, singhara and seasonal fruit are offered. Weddings, housewarmings and new ventures resume from this day, and Tulsi Vivah is kept this evening or the next. Maharashtra's Kartiki Ekadashi draws pilgrims to Pandharpur.
rule: Dev Uthani Ekadashi (Prabodhini) falls on Kartik Shukla Ekadashi (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Ekadashi rule with Smarta and Vaishnava dates. Shukla paksha, so Purnimanta and Amanta agree. Chaturmas began on Devshayani Ekadashi in Ashadha.

name: Tulsi Vivah
what: Tulsi Vivah on Kartik Shukla Dwadashi is the ceremonial wedding of the tulsi plant to Vishnu in his shaligram or Krishna form, opening the wedding season. The tulsi pot is decorated as a bride with a red cloth, bangles and a sugarcane mandap, the shaligram or image is brought as the groom in the evening, and the household performs the marriage rites with mangalashtak, the tying of the knot, kanyadan and a feast of puffed rice, sugarcane, amla and tamarind. Some families keep it on Ekadashi evening or on Kartik Purnima instead.
rule: Tulsi Vivah falls on Kartik Shukla Dwadashi (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Udaya rule on Dwadashi; several almanacs place the wedding on Ekadashi evening (pradosh) or on Purnima, so the owner's family custom may differ by a day. Shukla paksha, so Purnimanta and Amanta agree.

name: Kartik Purnima (Dev Deepawali)
what: Kartik Purnima, or Dev Deepawali and Tripuri Purnima, is the full Moon of Kartik and the end of the month-long Kartik bathing. The day begins with a river bath, Vishnu worship and gifts; in the evening the ghats of Varanasi are lit with a million lamps as the gods' own Diwali, and lamps are floated on rivers everywhere. Shiva's victory over Tripurasura, the Matsya avatar and Kartikeya's birth are all placed today. Sikhs keep Guru Nanak's birthday on this Purnima, Pushkar's camel fair ends, and Jains gather at Palitana as the pilgrimage season opens.
rule: Kartik Purnima (Dev Deepawali) falls on Kartik Shukla Purnima (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Udaya rule. Purnima is the same civil date in Purnimanta and Amanta. Guru Nanak Jayanti follows the same tithi.

name: Karthigai Deepam
what: Karthigai Deepam is the Tamil festival of lamps on the day of Krittika (Karthigai) nakshatra in the solar month Karthigai, close to the full Moon. Every home lights rows of clay lamps (agal vilakku) at dusk on the doorstep, balcony and puja room, and offers pori (puffed rice) and appam. At Tiruvannamalai the great Mahadeepam is lit on top of Arunachala hill in a copper cauldron with tonnes of ghee, visible for miles, and the ten-day Brahmotsavam ends there. Kerala keeps the same night as Thrikkarthika for Bhagavathy with lamps.
rule: Karthigai Deepam (observed in the south) is the day in the solar month of Vrishchika whose sunrise has Krittika nakshatra; when two days qualify, the one with more daylight under that nakshatra is taken.
conventionNote: Nakshatra rule in a solar month: the day in Karthigai (Sun in Vrishchika) whose daylight is mostly under Krittika, taking the passage nearest the full Moon if there are two. Listed under the South region. Also called Bharani Deepam the day before at Tiruvannamalai.

name: Kalabhairav Jayanti
what: Kalabhairav Jayanti, or Bhairava Ashtami, on Margashirsha Krishna Ashtami marks the appearance of Shiva as Kala Bhairava, the keeper of time and of Kashi. The worship is done at night with lamps, sesame-oil, black cloth and offerings of mustard oil, urad dal and coconut; dogs, Bhairava's companions, are fed. The Kala Bhairava temple of Varanasi and Ujjain's Kal Bhairav temple hold all-night festivals, and the Bhairava Ashtakam of Shankara is recited. Many keep a fast through the day and a vigil through the night.
rule: Kalabhairav Jayanti falls on Margashirsha Krishna Ashtami (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Nishita rule: the civil day whose midnight falls inside Ashtami. Krishna paksha: Margashirsha in Purnimanta is Kartik in Amanta; the civil date is the same.

name: Utpanna Ekadashi
what: Utpanna Ekadashi is the dark-fortnight Ekadashi of Margashirsha, remembered as the day the goddess Ekadashi herself appeared from Vishnu to overcome the demon Mura; those beginning the yearly Ekadashi vow traditionally start with this one. The grain fast, bath, Vishnu worship with tulsi and lamp and a day of reading or japa follow the common pattern; the Bhavishyottara Purana tells the story. Parana is the next morning inside the Dwadashi tithi after Hari Vasara has ended. Falling in the first cool weeks of winter, it is kept with warm gifts of blankets and sesame sweets.
rule: Utpanna Ekadashi falls on Margashirsha Krishna Ekadashi (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Ekadashi rule with Smarta and Vaishnava dates. Krishna paksha: Margashirsha in Purnimanta is Kartik in Amanta; the civil date is the same.

name: Vivah Panchami
what: Vivah Panchami on Margashirsha Shukla Panchami is the wedding anniversary of Rama and Sita. Janakpur in Nepal, Sita's home, and Ayodhya re-enact the marriage with a procession of the groom's party, the garland exchange and the wedding rites before the temple images, with the Ramcharitmanas Balkand read through the day. Rama temples everywhere dress the images as bride and groom in the evening, and families keep the day with a reading, a fast until the evening puja and a shared meal. Some communities avoid holding their own weddings on this date, out of regard for Sita's hard life after hers.
rule: Vivah Panchami falls on Margashirsha Shukla Panchami (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Udaya rule. Shukla paksha, so Purnimanta and Amanta agree.

name: Gita Jayanti (Mokshada Ekadashi)
what: Gita Jayanti on Margashirsha Shukla Ekadashi, the Mokshada Ekadashi, is the day Krishna spoke the Bhagavad Gita to Arjuna at Kurukshetra. Temples and homes read all eighteen chapters through the day, often in group recitation; Kurukshetra holds a week-long festival with a Gita yagna and deepdan on the Brahma Sarovar, and ISKCON temples run Gita exams and lectures. The Ekadashi fast is kept as usual, with a lamp offered to the Gita itself, and parana follows the next morning inside the Dwadashi after Hari Vasara.
rule: Gita Jayanti (Mokshada Ekadashi) falls on Margashirsha Shukla Ekadashi (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Ekadashi rule (Smarta sunrise tithi, later day when doubled, Vaishnava a day later when Dashami touches dawn). Shukla paksha, so Purnimanta and Amanta agree. The engine lists this one entry for both Gita Jayanti and Mokshada Ekadashi.

name: Dattatreya Jayanti
what: Dattatreya Jayanti on Margashirsha Purnima marks the birth of Dattatreya, the combined form of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, at dusk. Datta temples at Ganagapur, Narasobawadi, Audumbar and Mahur hold their yearly festivals with the Gurucharitra read over seven days ending today; the image is bathed and dressed in the evening, the Datta Bavani and Datta Stotra are sung, and a fast is kept until the evening puja. The day is central to Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat and Andhra, and is also kept by followers of the Swami Samarth and Gajanan Maharaj traditions.
rule: Dattatreya Jayanti falls on Margashirsha Shukla Purnima (Purnimanta month name), on the day that tithi covers the evening (pradosh kala, the first tenth of the night).
conventionNote: Pradosh rule: the day on which Purnima runs in the evening after sunset, since the birth is placed at dusk. Purnima is the same civil date in Purnimanta and Amanta.

name: Saphala Ekadashi
what: Saphala Ekadashi is the dark-fortnight Ekadashi of Pausha, the first Ekadashi of the civil year in most years. The grain fast, bath, Vishnu worship with tulsi, fruit and a lamp kept through the night, and a day of reading or japa follow the common pattern; the Brahmanda Purana tells its story through prince Lumpaka. Seasonal fruit such as coconut, pomegranate and amla is offered. Parana is the next morning inside the Dwadashi tithi after Hari Vasara has ended. Saphala means fruitful, and the day is remembered for gifts of winter fruit and warm clothing.
rule: Saphala Ekadashi falls on Pausha Krishna Ekadashi (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Ekadashi rule with Smarta and Vaishnava dates. Krishna paksha: Pausha in Purnimanta is Margashirsha in Amanta; the civil date is the same.

name: Pausha Putrada Ekadashi
what: Pausha Putrada Ekadashi is the bright-fortnight Ekadashi of Pausha, the second Putrada Ekadashi of the year after the one in Shravana, kept by couples hoping for a child and by anyone keeping the yearly round. The grain fast, bath, Vishnu worship with tulsi and lamp and a day of reading or japa follow the common pattern; the Bhavishya Purana tells its story through king Suketuman. Parana is the next morning inside the Dwadashi tithi, after Hari Vasara and before a fifth of the day has passed. In the south it is called Vaikuntha Ekadashi.
rule: Pausha Putrada Ekadashi falls on Pausha Shukla Ekadashi (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Ekadashi rule with Smarta and Vaishnava dates. Shukla paksha, so Purnimanta and Amanta agree; the Amanta month is also Pausha (Margazhi in Tamil, hence Vaikuntha Ekadashi at Srirangam).

name: Pausha Purnima
what: Pausha Purnima is the full Moon of Pausha, the day the month of Magha bathing (Magha snan) begins at Prayagraj, Haridwar and Varanasi and the kalpavasis take up their month-long stay on the river bank. The day is kept with a bath at dawn, Vishnu and Sun worship, gifts of sesame, blankets and warm food in the cold, and the Satyanarayan story in the evening. Chhattisgarh marks Chherchhera, when children collect grain from house to house, and the Shakambhari Navratri ends on this Purnima in some traditions.
rule: Pausha Purnima falls on Pausha Shukla Purnima (Purnimanta month name), on the day whose sunrise has that tithi.
conventionNote: Udaya rule. Purnima is the same civil date in Purnimanta and Amanta; it opens Magha in the Purnimanta count, so the month of bathing runs to Magha Purnima.
